progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c08a (class rule, [O], acidified potassium dichromate orange to green, distil for the aldehyde, reflux with excess for the acid, secondary to ketone, tertiary stays orange, the green colour shows oxidation not the product, chromium(VI) hazard stated once). chem-m7-c08b (aldehyde and ketone structures and names; Tollens' silver mirror, Fehling's or Benedict's brick-red, both only with the aldehyde; dichromate test; the flow "oxidise, distil, test the product"; Tollens' made fresh). skills-s07 and chem-m7-p03 (validity, reliability, accuracy; word, feature, fix; hazard, harm, control). chem-m7-p01 (the organic waste container; GHS codes on a risk table). chem-m6 (litmus: blue turns red in acid). Year 11: distillation and reflux apparatus from c06 and c08a plates.
progression.startsWith: Choose an oxidation and collection method. The video opens: Warm three alcohols with acidified dichromate, and two of them turn it green. That tells you something was oxidised. It doesn't tell you what formed: an aldehyde, a ketone and an acid can all come from the same orange solution.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the aim; choosing a fair set of alcohols and a control; sorting alcohols by the dichromate colour; naming the independent, dependent and controlled variables; choosing distillation or reflux for each product and explaining why; predicting each distillate's test results; explaining why the distillate, not the flask, is tested, and how known samples, repeats and the distilling temperature support the conclusion; writing the risk rows for chromium(VI), the acids, the alcohols and products, Tollens' reagent and hot glassware, with disposal.
progression.nextLesson: carboxylic acids (route chem-m7-c09, "Why are carboxylic acids acidic?").

teaching.task: Warm an alcohol with acidified dichromate and it turns green. That shows something was oxidised, but what did you actually make? How do you make, collect and test the products of primary and secondary alcohols so the evidence points to one answer, and do it safely?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) green shows oxidation, not the product (1); (2) the aim and a fair set of alcohols, plus a control (2); (3) part A sorts the alcohols: primary and secondary green, tertiary and water orange (3); (4) one variable changed, the rest kept the same (4); (5) distil as it forms to catch the aldehyde, because it boils far below the alcohol and leaves before further oxidation; the distilling temperature supports the identification (5); (6) reflux with excess oxidant reaches the acid because the condenser returns the aldehyde to the oxidant (6); (7) the secondary alcohol gives a ketone that dichromate doesn't oxidise further (7); (8) each product has its own test pattern (8); (9) test the distillate, not the flask, and run known samples: validity (9); (10) repeats agree: reliability; matching known samples and boiling temperatures supports the identification: accuracy; a faint acid result in the aldehyde sample is an investigation prompt on screen, not a spoken diagnosis (10); (11) the hazards and their controls (11); memory aid (12); attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: warm three alcohols with acidified dichromate and two turn it green, which shows something was oxidised but not what formed, so the practical asks how to make, collect and test each product so the evidence points to one answer, and do it safely. The aim uses propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, which share a formula so only the position of the OH differs, with 2-methylpropan-2-ol as the tertiary comparison and a water-only tube as the control. In part A the teacher demonstrates a warm water bath test that sorts the alcohols by whether the dichromate turns green, and the variables card names the alcohol's class, the observations and what stays the same. In part B the aldehyde is caught by distilling straight away, because propanal boils about fifty degrees below the alcohol and escapes before it is oxidised again; reflux with excess oxidant takes the primary alcohol on to propanoic acid; propan-2-ol gives propanone. Tollens' and Benedict's respond only to the aldehyde and blue litmus only to the acid. Testing the distillate, not the flask, is the validity point, because the flask holds sulfuric acid and chromium ions; repeats and known samples support reliability and accuracy, and the risk table centres on chromium(VI). The memory aid is green says oxidised, the test says what. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Warm three alcohols with acidified dichromate, and two of them turn it green. That tells you something was oxidised. It doesn't tell you what formed: an aldehyde, a ketone and an acid can all come from the same orange solution. Here you'll make each product, collect it and test it, so the evidence points to one answer.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "In a teacher demonstration, propan-1-ol was heated with excess acidified potassium dichromate under reflux for 20 minutes. The flask was cooled and a strip of blue litmus paper was dipped into the reaction mixture. The litmus turned red, and a student concluded that propanoic acid had formed. Explain why this conclusion is not valid, and describe how the method should be changed to give a valid conclusion." Tests the validity move (the flask contains sulfuric acid). Answer: the acidified dichromate contains sulfuric acid, which turns litmus red whether or not propanoic acid formed, so the test does not measure the product; distil off the product and test the distillate (and/or test a blank of acidified dichromate treated the same way). Crossed mistake: "repeat the litmus test several times" (repeats check reliability, not validity; s07's word, feature, fix). (A2) "Pentan-2-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol were each warmed with acidified potassium dichromate solution. Each mixture was then distilled, and the distillate was warmed with freshly prepared Tollens' reagent. Predict the observations for each alcohol, name any organic product, and explain the observations." Tests the class rule and the test's reason with new alcohols (C₅). Answer: pentan-2-ol is secondary: orange to green; product pentan-2-one; no silver mirror (a ketone has no H on its carbonyl carbon). 2-methylbutan-2-ol is tertiary: stays orange (no H on the C–OH carbon), no oxidation product; its distillate is unreacted alcohol, so no mirror. Crossed mistake: "pentan-2-ol: green, so a silver mirror" (green does not mean aldehyde).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the products of the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols" "describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)" (carried by the risk table, route review change 5) this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the investigation; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: the aim; the choice of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol (isomers, so only the position of the OH differs) with 2-methylpropan-2-ol as the tertiary comparison and a water-only tube as the control; part A, a water-bath test that sorts the alcohols by whether they turn acidified dichromate green; the variables and the control; part B, making each product: distil the primary alcohol's product as it forms (aldehyde), reflux the primary alcohol with excess oxidant then distil a sample (acid), and distil the secondary alcohol's product (ketone); testing each distillate with Tollens' reagent, Benedict's (or Fehling's) solution and blue litmus, against known samples (glucose for the aldehyde tests, dilute acid for litmus, water for no change); why the distillate is tested, not the flask (validity); repeats and agreement (reliability); matching results to known samples and the distilling temperature (accuracy of the identification); the risk assessment and disposal. Recalled, not re-taught: why oxidation needs an H on the C–OH carbon, why the aldehyde distils off, why reflux reaches the acid (c08a); why only the aldehyde gives a mirror or a brick-red solid (c08b); validity, reliability, accuracy and word, feature, fix (skills-s07, chem-m7-p03). Not here: the dichromate half-equations and balanced redox equations (c08a author note d); acidified permanganate as the oxidant (a grey tag only in the risk scene); carboxylic acid properties and the sodium carbonate test (chem-m7-c09); yields and purification; infrared or mass spectra (Module 8); multi-step synthesis (c13, g03).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c08a and c08b: dichromate orange and chromium(III) green as painted in the plates; aldehyde –CHO and ketone C=O navy; OH ringed red; the three alcohols in fixed colours across tags, table rows and chips (propan-1-ol teal, propan-2-ol violet, 2-methylpropan-2-ol grey-blue, water control plain grey); hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant, as chem-m7-p03): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus plate; the right third holds the current card (method step, variables, evidence table, validity card, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends. Plates and owner rules: no people or hands (liquids are added by coded dropper outlines and coded pours; flames are absent by design); apparatus (reflux and distillation set-ups, test tubes in racks, water bath, litmus, bottles) as painted plates, listed by filename, never stretched; molecules coded in the c08a style; at most about three bright text items; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (about 15 to 30 s) with one crossed-out mistake; original HSC-style questions only; real GHS classifications; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims; optional key notes hold. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The orange dichromate plate cross-fades to green as three product chips write in a row beneath it; the aim line writes and the two propanol structures draw side by side with their OH ringed, then shrink to name chips; the water-bath plate pair cross-fades from before to after and each tube's tag gains a result chip; the variables card writes one row per cue; the distillation plate takes the centre with a distillate tag and a boiling point strip, then the reflux plate runs its vapour return loop, then the distillation plate returns with the propan-2-ol chip and its equation; the evidence table writes one column per test with small result thumbnails; the flask against distillate split shows litmus turning red in the flask; the reliability and accuracy cards write small; the risk table shows one spoken row at a time; the memory line writes over a green tube and a mini evidence table; each attempt clears the board with its question card, and its feedback underlines the card as a chip writes and a crossed trap lands; the three-row decision card lights on cue; scene crossfade with settle.
